content: This is an updated version of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2013. Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological condition that affects approximately 0.5% to 1% of the population. While pharmacological treatments are the primary approach to managing epilepsy, about 30% of individuals do not respond adequately to these therapies and fail to achieve seizure remission. Experimental and clinical evidence suggests that activation of inflammatory pathways plays a role in the development of epilepsy. This has led to the hypothesis that targeting these pathways with immunomodulatory interventions could represent a novel therapeutic strategy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of immunomodulatory interventions in reducing seizures, as well as their impact on adverse effects, cognitive function, and quality of life, compared to placebo, when used as an additional therapy for focal epilepsy in both children and adults. For this update, a comprehensive search of databases was conducted on November 11, 2021. The databases included the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and Medline (Ovid), covering studies from 1946 to November 10, 2021. CRS Web encompasses randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials from sources such as PubMed, EMBASE, ClinicalTrials.gov, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and the Specialized Registers of Cochrane Review Groups, including Epilepsy. No language restrictions were applied. Bibliographies of retrieved studies were also reviewed to identify additional relevant studies. The review included randomized, placebo-controlled trials of add-on immunomodulatory drug interventions. These trials required adequate methods of randomization concealment and could be double-blind, single-blind, or unblinded. Eligible participants were children (aged over 2 years) and adults diagnosed with focal epilepsy. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. The primary outcomes assessed were: (1) a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, (2) seizure freedom, (3) treatment withdrawal for any reason, (4) quality of life, and (5) adverse effects. Analyses were conducted using an intention-to-treat (ITT) approach, and results were presented as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The review included three randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials involving a total of 172 participants. These trials included both children and adults with focal epilepsy, with treatment phases lasting six weeks and follow-up periods ranging from six weeks to six months. One trial adequately described its method of randomization concealment, while the other two were rated as having unclear risk of bias due to insufficient reporting of study design details. All three trials reported effective blinding. Analyses were conducted on an ITT basis. One trial was sponsored by the manufacturer of an immunomodulatory agent, introducing a high risk of funding bias. Immunomodulatory interventions were found to be significantly more effective than placebo in reducing seizure frequency, with a risk ratio (RR) of 2.30 (95% CI 1.15 to 4.60; 3 studies, 172 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). However, there was insufficient evidence to determine whether participants were more likely to discontinue immunomodulatory treatment compared to placebo (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.28 to 3.80; 3 studies, 172 participants; low-certainty evidence). The risk ratio for adverse effects was 1.16 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.59; 1 study, 66 participants; low-certainty evidence). Adverse effects such as dizziness, headache, fatigue, and gastrointestinal disturbances were more frequently associated with immunomodulatory interventions. There was limited to no data available on the cognitive effects or quality of life outcomes. No significant heterogeneity was observed between the studies for any of the outcomes. The overall certainty of the evidence, assessed using the GRADE approach, was judged to be low to moderate. This was due to potential attrition bias from missing outcome data and imprecise results with wide confidence intervals. In conclusion, immunomodulatory interventions as an add-on treatment for children and adults with focal epilepsy appear to be effective in reducing seizure frequency. However, it is not possible to draw definitive conclusions about the tolerability of these agents in this population. Further randomized controlled trials are necessary to provide more robust evidence.
